name: J04 — reconnect, both clients, one product
about: The reconnect dimension, driven by an ACTUAL severed connection: a relay
sits between the clients and the product and drops every socket it holds.
The server never moves.
Why a relay and not a restart: the product admits only an ephemeral port
(`IA0-1R admits only --port 0`), so restarting it returns a DIFFERENT
endpoint. A client handed a new address would be exercising configuration,
not recovery. (An earlier revision of this file described a stop/restart on
a fixed port; that was never what the step did.)
WHAT EACH POST-CUT OBSERVATION PROVES, stated because they prove different
things and one of them proves less than it looks:
1. `before the cut` still on screen — the old transcript SURVIVED, with no
duplicate of it. On its own this proves almost NOTHING about recovery: a
client that died quietly and kept its last frame would satisfy it. It is
retained as the no-loss/no-duplication check it always was, not as
evidence of reconnection.
2. A FRESH prompt answered after the cut — the client can still transact
with the product. This proves the request path recovered. It does NOT
prove the event subscription did: an answer can arrive through durable
history polling alone.
3. The native client showing a RUNNING execution during that fresh turn —
this is the one that proves resubscription. `running` can only come from
a live `session.execution.started`; it is not in the durable re-list, so
a client reconciling from history alone can never display it. The
retained client has no marker here that I can assert with the same
confidence, so its post-cut evidence stops at (2) and is reported as
that rather than dressed up as more.
THE POST-CUT TURN IS DELIBERATELY SLOW. Step 21 asserts the native client
shows a LIVE execution after the connection was cut and remade, and a turn
that answers in two fragments is over before either client's screen can be
read — the assertion then depends on winning a race against a fixture,
which is not what this scenario is about. Measured: it passed, and then
began failing when the scripted provider got faster, on a client that had
not changed. Asking for a slow count keeps the live state observable for
as long as the observation needs.
